entity_name: Road from London through Barnet to the fork (Great North Road)
value_text: Road from London through Barnet to the fork (Great North Road)
detail: The main road north from London climbed Barnet Hill, ran through the market town past its chapel, and crossed Hadley Green to a fork where the Hadley Highstone now stands. Both armies came this way.

entity_name: St Albans road (now Kitts End Road)
value_text: St Albans road (now Kitts End Road)
detail: The road from London to St Albans, the Midlands and the north-west: the left-hand branch at the fork, running north-west past Kitts End to Dancers Hill. In 1471 this was the great road, and Warwick's army had marched down it from St Albans; today it is a country lane.

entity_name: Hatfield road (later the Great North Road)
value_text: Hatfield road (later the Great North Road)
detail: The right-hand branch at the fork, heading north-east to Potters Bar, Hatfield and the north along the edge of Enfield Chase.

entity_name: Wood Street (road west to Barnet Common)
value_text: Wood Street (road west to Barnet Common)
detail: The lane branching west at Barnet chapel, widening as a drove towards Barnet Common.

entity_name: Lane from the green to Hadley church
value_text: Lane from the green to Hadley church
detail: A lane from the main road across the east side of the green to the church at the edge of Enfield Chase.

A small stream rising north of Hadley church and running east through a shallow valley inside Enfield Chase. One contemporary newsletter puts Edward's army in a hollow or marsh; this valley is the usual candidate.

entity_name: Stream at the head of Margery Mead
value_text: Stream at the head of Margery Mead
detail: A stream falling north-west from the Kitts End side of the ridge into the broad, flat valley called Margery Mead, which may have been marshy before modern drainage.

The bank and hedge that divided Enfield Chase from the commons outside it, running north from Hadley towards Potters Bar beside the Hatfield road. If it was still a substantial hedged bank in 1471 it would have been a serious obstacle on the east side of the field.

entity_name: A possible 'hedge-side' on the Hadley Green interpretation
value_text: A possible 'hedge-side' on the Hadley Green interpretation
detail: The Arrivall says Warwick's men were drawn up 'under a hedge-side' rather more than half a mile from Barnet. On the Hadley Green interpretation that hedge ran east–west near the north edge of the green; A. H. Burne thought he could identify it beside Old Fold.

entity_name: Edge of the closes north of Kicks End Common
value_text: Edge of the closes north of Kicks End Common
detail: Hedged closes lay north of the common by 1479. The survey report's simplest reading of the sources puts Warwick's line behind this boundary, facing south across the common, with a frontage of about 650 m between the two roads.

entity_name: Edge of the Old Fold estate beside the green
value_text: Edge of the Old Fold estate beside the green
detail: Old Fold was a compact, fully hedged estate when first mapped in 1726, with its moated house at the eastern edge next to Hadley Green.

entity_name: Chapel of St John the Baptist, Chipping Barnet
value_text: Chapel of St John the Baptist, Chipping Barnet
detail: The town's church, standing at the angle where Wood Street leaves the High Street on the crest of the ridge, about 400 ft (122 m) above sea level. A chapel of St John is recorded here in 1361; it was largely rebuilt in the first half of the 15th century and was treated as a parish church by the time of the battle.

The parish church of Hadley, on the plateau at the edge of Enfield Chase east of the green. Hadley is listed as a parish church about 1175 and a hermitage 'in the park of Hadley' is recorded about 1136. The church that stood here on the day of the battle was replaced about 1494 by the present building, which carries that date on its west tower.

A moated manor house at the north-west corner of Hadley Green, held by the Frowyk family of London merchants from soon after 1271 until 1527. A manor house is mentioned in 1310 and three sides of its moat survive beside the golf club house. It was certainly standing in 1471 and, on the Hadley Green interpretation, lay in or just behind Warwick's line.

entity_name: Chapel for the dead of the battle (site not proven)
value_text: Chapel for the dead of the battle (site not proven)
detail: The Great Chronicle of London (about 1512) says the common dead were buried on the plain and that a little chapel was afterwards built there to remember their souls. A will suggests it was still in use in 1519–20; by Stow's day it had become a house. Since 1970 it has been identified with 'the Hermitage', a moated site on the former Kicks End Common, one arm of whose moat survives as a pond.

The area registered as the battlefield by English Heritage in 1995, following a National Army Museum report: Hadley Green, Old Fold and the ground north of Monken Hadley. Its northern edge is a little over half a mile from Barnet, matching the Arrivall's distance.

entity_name: Kitts End: the 2015–18 survey's alternative site
value_text: Kitts End: the 2015–18 survey's alternative site
detail: The former Kicks End Common and its surroundings, between the St Albans and Hatfield roads north of the fork: a level hilltop of open common, about 1.9 km from the Barnet boundary, edged by hedged closes on the north and the bank of Enfield Chase on the east, with the Monken Mead valley falling away to the south-east. The survey report judged that this ground 'most closely' fits the written accounts, and the putative battle chapel lies on it.

Stand-in for the western wing of Warwick's army, which the sources agree overlapped and routed the king's left; its men chased the fugitives towards Barnet and, returning in the mist, were taken for enemies by their own side. That the Earl of Oxford led the attack is attested; that this was the 'right wing' is inference.

Stand-in for the middle of Warwick's line. Modern accounts put John Neville, Marquess Montagu, here and Warwick himself with a reserve behind; no contemporary source says where either stood. Both were killed.
Stand-in for the eastern wing of Warwick's army, which the king's line overlapped. The Duke of Exeter was badly wounded and left for dead; his place on the left is a modern inference.
Stand-in for the western end of the king's line, which was overlapped, broken and driven back through Barnet towards London. Lord Hastings led the rearward, which later sources place here.
Stand-in for the king's own division. The Arrivall, written by a servant of the king, describes Edward fighting in the midst of the press.
Stand-in for the eastern end of the king's line, which overlapped the enemy's. Richard, Duke of Gloucester, aged eighteen, led the vanguard, conventionally placed on the right.

A crossing of the Thames by wading. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle has Edmund 'go over at Brentford' and later 'ford over the Thames at Brentford' in 1016, so a usable ford existed. The county history thinks the lowest permanent ford on the Thames was probably at Old England, the low ground by the Brent mouth; that is where it is drawn.
The tributary that gives Brentford its name, joining the Thames from the north. Alluvium lies along it and at its mouth.

entity_name: Crossing of the Brent on the west road
value_text: Crossing of the Brent on the west road
detail: Where the road west from London crossed the Brent. The name Brentford, recorded from 705, is usually taken to mean this ford. A bridge is first recorded in 1224, long after this window, so a ford is shown.

entity_name: Road from London (later Brentford High Street)
value_text: Road from London (later Brentford High Street)
detail: The main road from London to the west, successor to the Roman road to Silchester, running along the gravel just above the Thames to the Brent crossing.
The same road beyond the Brent, through the later Brentford End towards Hounslow and Staines. The county history calls the London to Staines road probably the oldest man-made feature of the district.
A way from the west road to the head of the Thames ford, keeping west and south of the Brent's last bend.
Ploughed strips on the brickearth and gravel above the road, standing for the farmland of the bishop of London's manor.
Ploughed strips south of the west road, standing for the large arable of the manor of Isleworth, which Domesday Book credits with land for 55 ploughs.
A few small boats off Old Brentford. A Thames fishery at Brentford existed by 996, when the king granted half of it to Winchester; later records speak of weirs.
A shaded band over the ford as drawn: one place where Edmund's army may have crossed the Thames in 1016.
A second shaded band, on the line of the later Kew ferry from Old Brentford, shown to make plain that the crossing place is not known.

A shaded area on the Surrey bank where the Danish army may have stood. The Chronicle's wording, that Edmund crossed and then fought, is usually read as putting the fight south of the river, and the county history (citing Stenton) says it was fought on the south bank.
A block of plain figures at the Middlesex end of the ford, standing for the English army that crossed the Thames here under King Edmund in 1016.

entity_name: Englishmen ahead of the army (stand-in figures)
value_text: Englishmen ahead of the army (stand-in figures)
detail: A small loose group on the Surrey bank, standing for the men who, the Chronicle says, 'went before the main army with a design to plunder' and of whom many drowned.
A block of plain figures on the Surrey bank, standing for the Danish army that Edmund fought and put to flight.
A timber bridge across the Thames on the Fish Street Hill line, the reason the town stood here. A probable timber pier base of the late 1st century was excavated near Pudding Lane in 1981.
The first civic centre on Cornhill: a gravelled court with a basilica about 40 × 20 m. It stayed in use while the much larger second forum was built around it.
The great forum-basilica of Londinium, built around and over the first forum from about 100 CE; the basilica ran along its north side.
An oval arena beneath today's Guildhall Yard: built in timber about 74 CE and rebuilt shortly after 120 with a masonry arena wall and entrances. The seating was always timber.
An earth-and-timber fort of about 1.5 hectares built on Cornhill around 63 CE, soon after the Boudican revolt: the main physical evidence for the town's military-led recovery.

A stone-walled fort of about 4.5 hectares on the north-west edge of the town, built about 120. It was probably out of use as a fort by the later 2nd century; its north and west walls were built into the city wall about 200.
The landward wall, about 3 km long, 2–2.6 m thick and about 6.4 m high, built of Kentish ragstone c. 190–225 and enclosing some 134 hectares. It set the limits of the city for the next 1,400 years.

A wall about 1,700 m long added along the river front c. 255–275 on the line of Thames Street, closing the circuit. Its eastern end was strengthened as late as c. 388–402, parts still stood in the late 9th century, and it had gone by the 12th.
A large terraced riverside complex with courts and an ornamental pool under Cannon Street station, formerly called the governor's palace.
A large public bath-house terraced into the hillside above the river.
A small aisled temple on the east bank of the Walbrook, built c. 240–250 with its apse to the west; converted, probably to Bacchus, in the early 4th century. Found in 1954.

entity_name: Road to the bridge from the south (Borough High Street line)
value_text: Road to the bridge from the south (Borough High Street line)
detail: The approach road across the Southwark islands, where the roads from the Kent coast and the south met before the bridge.
The road from the bridge past the forum and north towards Lincoln and York.
The principal street of Londinium, running east–west north of the Walbrook crossing.
The market street ('ceap') of the re-established Saxon city, the spine of the medieval street plan.
The Roman road west from Newgate towards Silchester, still a main road in 1625.
The road along the river terrace from Ludgate through Lundenwic to Westminster.
The stream that divided the Roman and medieval city. Progressively built over and culverted; gone from view by the late 16th century.
A tributary entering the Thames at Blackfriars; an open, increasingly foul river throughout this period.
A cathedral has stood on Ludgate Hill since 604. The medieval building, 'Old St Paul's', was one of the longest churches in Europe and carried a very tall timber spire until 1561.

A trading shore from the late 880s ('Æthelred's Hythe', first charter 889): at first an open beach market, with low timber revetments from the late 10th century and embankments dated 1021 and 1045. The main dock above the bridge through the Middle Ages.

entity_name: Late Saxon and Norman timber bridge
value_text: Late Saxon and Norman timber bridge
detail: A timber bridge existed again by about 1000 CE and was repaired or rebuilt several times before the stone bridge replaced it.

The stone bridge of 19 arches and a drawbridge opening, begun in 1176 and finished in 1209, about 276 m long and only about 6 m wide, lined with houses, with a chapel on its central pier and a fortified gate at the Southwark end.

Houses stood on the bridge from soon after it was finished: about 140 by 1358 and about 130 in the 16th century, overhanging the river on both sides of a roadway only about 4 m wide and bridging it in places.

entity_name: Chapel of St Thomas on the Bridge
value_text: Chapel of St Thomas on the Bridge
detail: A two-storey chapel on the large central pier, dedicated to Thomas Becket. Rebuilt 1387–96; closed in 1548 and turned into a house, shop and warehouse.
The fortified gate at the Southwark end of the bridge. After 1577 the heads of traitors were displayed here.
A gate tower beside the drawbridge, seventh opening from the Southwark end. Demolished in 1577 and replaced by Nonsuch House.

A four-and-a-half-storey timber house with corner turrets and onion domes, built across the bridge in 1577–79 on the site of the drawbridge tower; its design is attributed to Lewis Stockett, Surveyor of the Queen's Works.
Tide-driven waterwheels under the northernmost arches, set up by Peter Morris in 1581–82 to pump river water into the city.
The parish church at the north end of the bridge; every traveller crossing passed its door.
The riverside hall of the Fishmongers' Company, just upstream of the bridge, from 1434.
Church at the south bridge foot dedicated to St Olaf of Norway, in existence by the late 11th century.

Augustinian priory church at the Southwark bridge foot, refounded 1106, rebuilt in Gothic style after the fire of 1212. It became the parish church of St Saviour in 1540 and survives as Southwark Cathedral.
The London house of the bishops of Winchester on Bankside, with a great hall whose rose-window gable still stands.
The dock and market below the bridge, in use by about 1000 CE.
Massive oak-timber quays with open-fronted warehouses behind, rebuilt further out into the river several times between the 1st and 3rd centuries.

Edward the Confessor's great church, consecrated in 1065, was replaced from 1245 by Henry III's Gothic abbey. The nave took until the early 16th century; the west towers were not built until the 18th century and are not shown.
The Perpendicular Lady Chapel at the east end of Westminster Abbey.
William II's great hall of 1097–99, the largest in England, given its hammerbeam roof in the 1390s. The royal palace grew around it.

entity_name: Tower of London: the White Tower
value_text: Tower of London: the White Tower
detail: William the Conqueror's great stone keep in the south-east corner of the Roman walls, begun in the 1070s and complete by about 1100.

entity_name: Tower of London: inner curtain wall
value_text: Tower of London: inner curtain wall
detail: The towered inner curtain built mainly under Henry III.

entity_name: Tower of London: outer curtain and moat
value_text: Tower of London: outer curtain and moat
detail: Edward I's outer curtain wall and moat, 1275–85, which gave the Tower its concentric form.
A Norman castle in the south-west corner of the city, demolished in 1213; the site passed to the Blackfriars.
A great riverside house rebuilt after a fire in 1428 and remodelled as a royal residence by Henry VII about 1501.
The Knights Templar's church with its round nave, consecrated in 1185; the chancel was added by 1240.

The Dominican friary built from 1276 between Ludgate and the river; the city wall was moved west to enclose it. Dissolved 1538; its church was pulled down and the buildings became houses and, later, an indoor playhouse.
The Franciscan friary by Newgate. Its great 14th-century church, about 90 m long, became the parish church of Christ Church after the Dissolution.
The Augustinian friary founded in 1253. After 1538 the nave was given to London's Dutch Protestant community (1550).
A rich Augustinian priory founded in 1108 just inside Aldgate; the first London house to be dissolved (1532), then largely pulled down for a mansion.
Founded by Rahere in 1123 beside Smithfield. After the Dissolution the nave was demolished and the choir kept as a parish church.
A Carthusian monastery founded in 1371 with a great cloister of individual cells; a courtier's mansion after 1545 and Sutton's Hospital from 1611.
John of Gaunt's palace on the Strand, the grandest noble house in England, destroyed in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Henry VII's hospital was built on the ruins from 1505.
The city's great hall, rebuilt from 1411, standing over the buried Roman amphitheatre.
A quadrangular public granary and market built in the 1440s on the site of the Roman basilica.
Thomas Gresham's bourse, built 1566–68 around an arcaded courtyard on the Antwerp model and named the Royal Exchange after Elizabeth I's visit in 1571.
Henry VIII's brick palace beside the Fleet, built 1515–23; given to the City in 1553 as a workhouse and prison.
The archbishops of York's London house, seized by Henry VIII in 1529–30 and expanded into the largest palace in Europe, a sprawl of courts and galleries between the river and St James's Park.
Inigo Jones's Palladian hall of 1619–22, the first fully classical building in London. It replaced a banqueting house of 1606–07 that burned in January 1619.
Protector Somerset's Renaissance palace on the Strand, 1547–52; Denmark House under James I's queen.
A Jacobean courtyard mansion with corner turrets at Charing Cross, built about 1605–09 for the Earl of Northampton; known as Northumberland House only later.
The London residence of the archbishops of Canterbury since about 1200, on the marshy bank opposite Westminster.
A Cluniac priory (later abbey) founded in 1082 on the Bermondsey eyot; dissolved 1538 and replaced by a mansion.
The quay where duties were collected. A custom house stood at Wool Quay by 1377 and John Churchman built a new one in 1382.
The walled riverside base of the Hanseatic merchants, with its guildhall and warehouses. Its privileges were withdrawn in 1598 but the buildings stood.
Philip Henslowe's playhouse of 1587, the first on Bankside; its foundations were excavated in 1989.
Built about 1595 in Paris Garden; the subject of the only surviving sketch of an Elizabethan playhouse interior.
Built in 1599 from the timbers of the Theatre; burned on 29 June 1613 and rebuilt with a tiled roof by 1614.
A baiting ring on Bankside, replaced in 1613–14 by the Hope, a dual-purpose playhouse and baiting house.
The built-up river frontage of the City: successive timber and later stone revetments pushed the bank out into the Thames, creating wharves between Thames Street and the water.
The embanked south shore from Paris Garden past Winchester Palace to the bridge foot and St Olave's.
Sea-going and river vessels served the Roman port; wrecks of the period have been excavated at Blackfriars and County Hall.
The Thames was London's main highway. Period panoramas of the 16th and 17th centuries show it crowded with wherries and barges above the bridge and sea-going ships below it.

entity_name: Olaf's ships at the bridge (saga tradition)
value_text: Olaf's ships at the bridge (saga tradition)
detail: Longships below the timber bridge, standing for the saga account of an attack on London Bridge in 1014.

Five sarsen trilithons (ten uprights, five lintels) in a horseshoe about 13.7 m across, open to the north-east; the tallest, the Great Trilithon at the south-west, stood about 7 m above ground. Drawn from the stone catalogue: stone positions and sizes are surveyed from what stands today, the original complete form is reconstructed from them.

The outer ring of thirty sarsen uprights (about 4.1 m high, 2.1 m wide) carrying a continuous ring of thirty lintels about 4.9 m above ground; outer diameter about 29.6 m. Seventeen uprights and six lintels stand today. The complete ring shown in the built phases is a reconstruction.

On Parker Pearson's interpretation the 56 Aubrey Holes held bluestones from about 3000 BCE, so Stonehenge's first stones were a ring about 87 m across just inside the bank. Shown as 56 small standing bluestones.

entity_name: Q and R bluestone double arc (Stage 2)
value_text: Q and R bluestone double arc (Stage 2)
detail: A double ring of bluestones between the trilithons and the sarsen circle, set in the Q and R holes (paired 'dumbbell' sockets on the east, a single line on the south and west). Drawn as two parametric rings of 54 stones in all.

entity_name: Central bluestone circle (Stage 3) and bluestone oval (Stage 4)
value_text: Central bluestone circle (Stage 3) and bluestone oval (Stage 4)
detail: Two bluestone settings inside the trilithons, one after the other: a small central circle in Stage 3 and the oval of about 25 stones in Stage 4, which later became the horseshoe. Both are parametric stand-ins.

The bluestone circle between the trilithons and the sarsen circle, about 22 m across (radius 11 m), of 40-60 stones when complete (Stage 4). Nineteen stone positions are catalogued from the surviving stones and stumps; the complete ring is drawn as 60 parametric stones.

The bluestone horseshoe inside the trilithons, open to the north-east, of about 19 stones (Stage 5). Twelve positions are catalogued from surviving stones; the complete setting is drawn as 19 parametric stones.
A slab of green-grey sandstone about 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m at the foot of the Great Trilithon, from outside southern Britain. Drawn lying flat at ground level.
Four small sarsens (91-94) in a rectangle just inside the bank. Two (91, 93) survive; the other two positions are marked by modern plaques at the findspots of their barrows.
A fallen sarsen about 4.9 m long (6.1 m as catalogued when standing) in the north-east entrance, once standing there with companion stones D and E.
An unshaped sarsen about 4.7 m high, 77.4 m from the centre on the solstice axis, with a second stonehole (97) beside it.
Fifty-six chalk pits in a ring about 87 m across (circumference 271.6 m), just inside the bank, each about 1.06 m wide and 0.76 m deep on average. Cremations were inserted in their upper fills.

A circular bank with an external ditch, about 110 m across overall, with a wide entrance to the north-east on the solstice axis and a smaller one to the south. Ditch dug with antler picks; re-cut in Stage 3. Drawn with the ditch centreline at radius 53 m.

A computed marker for the Events menu: the direction of sunrise on the midsummer solstice seen from the centre of Stonehenge in 2500 BCE, azimuth 49.2 degrees. It is an analytical overlay, not a structure and not lighting. The lead computed the azimuth for 2500 BCE, latitude 51.179, obliquity 23.97 degrees, with the horizon assumed at 0.6 degrees.

A computed marker for the Events menu: the direction of sunset on the midwinter solstice seen from the centre of Stonehenge in 2500 BCE, azimuth 230 degrees. It is an analytical overlay, not a structure and not lighting. The lead computed the azimuth for 2500 BCE, latitude 51.179, obliquity 23.97 degrees, with the horizon assumed at 0.6 degrees.
A great banked and ditched enclosure about 2.75 km long and about 100 m wide, running ENE (bearing 84.6 degrees) north of Stonehenge, closed at both ends. Earlier than the stones.
A smaller banked and ditched enclosure about 420 m long and 40-60 m wide, running WSW-ENE about 750 m north-west of the west end of the Greater Cursus.
A long barrow just beyond the east end of the Greater Cursus, aligned north-south, about 62 x 20 m with ditches 11 m wide (as surveyed), levelled by ploughing and now under a track.
The Winterbourne Stoke Crossroads long barrow, 84 x 27 m and 3 m high, NE-SW, later the focus of a round-barrow cemetery.
A small long barrow on Normanton Down, mapped as a 19 x 9 m mound (bearing 11 degrees). Probably one of the two or three small long barrows EH and Internet Archaeology list here.
A long barrow on Normanton Down, 43 x 20 m and 2.3 m high, aligned west-east, with ditches about 4 m wide.
A long barrow near Normanton Down, 33 x 18 m and 1.6 m high, aligned NNW-SSE.

A processional way of two parallel banks with outside ditches, from the north-east entrance of Stonehenge along the solstice axis for about 530 m, then curving east across Stonehenge Bottom and King Barrow Ridge and down to the River Avon at West Amesbury, about 2.7 km in all. Built in Stage 3.

The largest henge in Britain: a circular enclosure about 500 m across with a huge outer bank about 3 m high and a deep ditch, built c. 2480-2450 BCE over the line of an earlier ring of timber posts, beside the Neolithic village on the slope to the Avon.

entity_name: Durrington Walls timber ring (beneath the later bank)
value_text: Durrington Walls timber ring (beneath the later bank)
detail: A great ring of up to about 300 timber posts, roughly 5 m apart, 440-450 m across, enclosing the valley and village before the henge bank was raised along the same line.
A circular setting of concentric rings of timber posts inside the henge, oriented to midwinter sunrise (south-east), beside the settlement.
A smaller timber circle found by Wainwright in 1966 just north of the Southern Circle.

entity_name: Woodhenge (six oval rings of timber posts)
value_text: Woodhenge (six oval rings of timber posts)
detail: Six concentric oval rings of timber posts (168 post-holes; outer ring 43 x 40 m), inside a ditch and bank 110 m across overall, with a single north-east entrance, near Durrington Walls.
The ditch (up to 12 m wide, 2.4 m deep) and bank (10 m wide, 1 m high) enclosing Woodhenge, 110 m across overall, with a north-east entrance.
An oval ditched enclosure about 45 x 55 m south-east of Stonehenge, excavated in the 1980s; the ditch was about 4 m wide and 3 m deep. Levelled by ploughing.
On the Avon bank at the end of the Avenue: a circle of about 25 stones (probably bluestones, from the shape of the sockets), later removed, then a small henge (ditch about 25 m across, outer bank).
A squat sarsen set up in a pit between Woodhenge and Durrington Walls, with cremations around it c. 2000 BCE. It lies fallen today.
A cemetery of round barrows on the ridge south of Stonehenge, burials roughly 2600-1600 BCE; about 35 survived in 1957. 33 round barrows are drawn.

entity_name: Old and New King Barrows (King Barrow Ridge)
value_text: Old and New King Barrows (King Barrow Ridge)
detail: Early Bronze Age round barrows along King Barrow Ridge, where the Avenue climbs the ridge (Old and New King Barrows together). 18 round barrows are drawn.
Round barrows along and around the Greater Cursus, including the one inside its west end and the Monarch of the Plain. 15 round barrows are drawn.
The round-barrow cemetery that grew up around the Winterbourne Stoke 1 long barrow at the crossroads west of Stonehenge. 18 round barrows are drawn.
A handful of round barrows on Stonehenge Down, south-west and north-west of the stones, some within the detailed district. 10 round barrows are drawn.
The Lake group of round barrows on the downs south of Normanton Down, at the southern edge of the modelled area. 16 round barrows are drawn.
The richest Early Bronze Age burial near Stonehenge (gold lozenge, daggers), c. 1950 BCE, 3.3 m high and 49 m across overall, excavated by Cunnington in 1808 (after the period shown).
9 isolated round barrows mapped across the landscape that belong to no named group (including the Coneybury Barrow and the Wilsford outlier).

An Iron Age hillfort of about 14 ha on a spur above the Avon, 730 m north-south, with a bank up to 40 m wide and 6 m above the ditch floor, a ditch 10 m wide and an outer counterscarp bank (defences 68 m wide in all).

A Benedictine nunnery said to be founded c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth; dissolved by Henry II in 1177 and refounded as a Fontevraud priory; dissolved at the Dissolution (1539 or 1540) and demolished, the estate going to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford.

entity_name: Parish church of St Mary and St Melor, Amesbury
value_text: Parish church of St Mary and St Melor, Amesbury
detail: The Grade I parish church of Amesbury, which may be the surviving priory church. It survived the demolition of the priory.
After the Dissolution the Crown granted the estate to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford, whose family held it until 1675. A Seymour house stood here in the 16th century.

The Hampshire (Wiltshire) Avon flowing south from Bulford past Durrington and Amesbury, round Vespasian's Camp and West Amesbury, about 10 km of the river within the modelled area. The Avenue ends on its bank at West Amesbury.

value_text: Roman building near the Cuckoo Stone

A Neolithic passage tomb on Anglesey under a mound about 26 m across, with a passage aligned on the midsummer sunrise. Cadw describes an earlier bank-and-ditch enclosure with a stone circle on the same spot.
A Neolithic passage tomb on the west coast of Anglesey. Several stones carry zig-zags and spirals like those in Irish tombs; Cadw notes Bryn Celli Ddu is the only other tomb in the UK with such art.
The best-preserved Neolithic portal dolmen in Wales: a capstone of about 16 tonnes on three uprights, once at the end of a cairn some 30 m long. Excavated by W. F. Grimes in 1936-7.

A stone-walled hillfort at about 480 m on Yr Eifl in Llŷn, crowded with some 150 round and sub-rectangular huts. Excavation shows it was probably built in the later Iron Age and stayed in use until at least the 4th century AD.

Bronze Age copper mines in the limestone of the Great Orme, with kilometres of tunnels dug with bone and stone tools. Nineteen radiocarbon dates span about 1700-900 BC; a 2019 study argues for a boom about 1600-1400 BC that supplied metal across Britain and as far as the Baltic.

A copper-bearing hill in north Anglesey. Hammerstones and charcoal found in old workings point to Early Bronze Age mining; Roman working is inferred from stamped copper ingots found on Anglesey and Pleiades lists it as a Roman mine.

A small lake in west Anglesey where more than 150 iron and bronze objects, including chariot fittings, swords, spearheads and slave chains, were found in peat in 1942-3 during airfield building. They are read as offerings made over several centuries.

A small inland promontory fort in north Pembrokeshire, about 88 by 74 m, excavated over many seasons. The main gateway was begun in the 5th century BC; occupation inside ended about the turn of the era, when a settlement was set up in the annexe.

One of three permanent legionary fortresses in Roman Britain, base of the Second Augustan Legion from about AD 75, with baths, barracks and an amphitheatre still visible. A Norman castle and small borough followed in the late 11th century.

The main Roman fort of north-west Wales, founded under Agricola about AD 77 for a 1,000-strong auxiliary regiment and linked by road to Chester and Caerleon. Coins show it was held until about 394, longer than any other fort in Wales.

The westernmost town of Roman Britain, Moridunum, capital of the Demetae, with an amphitheatre. A royal castle was founded on the Tywi in the early 12th century and the borough became the centre of English royal government in south-west Wales.
The Roman market town and administrative centre of the Silures, founded about AD 75-80. Its town walls, among the best preserved in northern Europe, still surround the village.
The only known Roman gold mine in Britain, at Pumsaint in Carmarthenshire: opencasts, adits and long aqueducts spread over at least a kilometre, beside a Roman fort.

A Roman auxiliary fort on the west bank of the river Neath. Excavation shows a first fort of about AD 75-80, a smaller one of 80-90 held until about 125, reoccupation from about 140 to 170 and a late military phase about 275-320.
A Roman fort guarding the Usk valley road, known as Gobannium. A Norman lord built a castle and priory here in the late 11th century and a walled market town grew beside them.

Site of an early legionary fortress, Burrium, built in the mid-50s AD during the war against the Silures and given up when the legion moved; Caerleon replaced it about AD 75. A Norman castle and planted borough followed in the 12th century.
A Roman auxiliary fort at Caerhun, guarding the crossing of the Conwy on the road from Chester to Caernarfon. It was occupied, with breaks, from Agricola’s campaign of AD 77/8 into the 4th century.
An upland Roman fort in Meirionnydd with a rare set of surrounding earthworks: a small amphitheatre, parade ground, bath-house and practice camps. A castle mound was later raised inside it.
A Roman fort west of Brecon, founded about AD 75 where two main roads met and garrisoned by a Spanish cavalry regiment, the Vettones.

The monastery founded by St David in the 6th century became the leading church of Wales and, under Norman bishops from 1115, a cathedral. The present church was begun in 1181; a 12th-century pope ruled two pilgrimages here equal to one to Rome, and Bishop Henry de Gower built the great palace in 1328-47.

Llanilltud Fawr, the monastery of St Illtud in the Vale of Glamorgan, was remembered as the great school of early Christian Wales; the 7th-century Life of St Samson is the earliest witness. Carved stones of the 9th-11th centuries commemorate kings of Glywysing.
A monastery founded by St Deiniol in the 6th century, the seat of the bishops of Gwynedd. The cathedral was rebuilt in stone in the 12th century and damaged in the wars of 1211, 1282 and 1402.
A church on the Taff associated with Saints Teilo, Dyfrig and Euddogwy. Bishop Urban began the present cathedral in 1120 and the Book of Llandaff was compiled to back its claims.

Twin hills above the Conwy estuary: by tradition the seat of Maelgwn, king of Gwynedd, in the 6th century. It was burnt by lightning in 812 and destroyed by the English in 822. Robert of Rhuddlan held it in the late 11th century; Henry III built a great castle in 1245-50, which Llywelyn ap Gruffudd destroyed in 1263.

A castle above the Tywi near Llandeilo, thought to have been founded in the later 12th century by the Lord Rhys and remembered as the principal court of Deheubarth. The standing remains are 13th and early 14th century.
An earthwork enclosure and mound on the river Banwy, named in later tradition as the chief court of the kings of Powys.

By tradition the chief seat of the kings of Gwynedd, on the west coast of Anglesey; the princes styled themselves ‘prince of Aberffraw’ in the 13th century. The settlement declined after a great storm in 1331 altered the coast.

A rocky stronghold above Nant Gwynant, the legendary site of Vortigern’s fortress and Merlin’s dragons. Excavations in 1910 and 1954-6 found Iron Age, Roman and early medieval occupation; a stone tower was added at the end of the 12th century.

The only crannog (artificial island) known in Wales, built in Llangorse Lake for the king of Brycheiniog from timbers felled between AD 889 and 893. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that a Mercian army sent by Æthelflæd destroyed ‘Brecenanmere’ in 916 and took the king’s wife captive.

A small defended hilltop near Cardiff, excavated by Leslie Alcock in the 1950s. Imported Mediterranean and Gaulish pottery, glass and fine metalworking show a wealthy household of the 5th to 7th centuries.

The shaft of a 9th-century cross near Llangollen, set up by Cyngen, king of Powys (died 854/5), in honour of his great-grandfather Eliseg. Its long Latin inscription, now illegible, traced the dynasty’s descent.

A castle on a cliff above the Wye, begun in 1067 by William fitz Osbern, earl of Hereford, and one of the first Norman strongholds in Wales. Its great tower is among the oldest stone castle buildings in Britain; a walled port town grew beside it.

A castle on a tidal promontory, established by the Normans about 1093-4 and never taken by the Welsh. The round great tower was built at the start of the 13th century; Henry Tudor, later Henry VII, was born here in 1457.

A series of Roman forts stood beside the Taff from the late 50s AD to the late 4th century. About 1081 William I set a castle inside the walls of the last fort, and the borough beside it became the head of the lordship of Glamorgan and one of the larger towns in Wales.
The largest castle in Wales, begun in 1268 by Gilbert de Clare, lord of Glamorgan, against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. Its concentric walls and wide artificial lakes were new to Britain.
A stone keep guarding a route through Snowdonia, built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, ruler of Gwynedd from 1201 to 1240. It fell to Edward I in 1283, who refitted it.

A castle on a rock in the Dysynni valley, begun in 1221 by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth to guard the southern border of Gwynedd. It was taken by Edward I’s forces in 1283 and given up after the Welsh rising of 1294.
A round stone tower at the foot of the Llanberis pass, most likely built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth in the late 12th or early 13th century.
A castle on a headland in Cardigan Bay. Llywelyn ap Iorwerth built the twin-towered gatehouse, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd added the outer ward, Edward I refitted it, and Owain Glyndŵr burnt it in 1404.
The first of Edward I’s castles in Wales, begun in 1277 and largely finished by 1284, with a planned borough beside it. Richard II met Henry Bolingbroke here in 1399.

The lowest crossing of the Clwyd. Edward the Elder founded a burh here in 921; it was Gruffudd ap Llywelyn’s seat until 1063; Robert of Rhuddlan raised a motte in 1073. Edward I began the present concentric castle in 1277 and issued the Statute of Rhuddlan here in 1284.

Edward I and Master James of St George built the castle and a 1.3 km circuit of town walls here between 1283 and 1287. The site had been the Cistercian abbey of Aberconwy, burial place of Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, which the king moved up the valley to Maenan.

Edward I began the castle and walled borough in 1283, with a quay, all at once; work lasted 47 years and was still unfinished about 1330. It was the centre of royal government in North Wales. The castle was in decay by the 16th century.

A concentric castle on a crag above Cardigan Bay, begun in May 1283 and largely complete by 1289. Owain Glyndŵr took it in 1404 and kept his court and family here until it was retaken in 1409; it fell again to the Yorkists in 1468 after a long siege.

The last of Edward I’s Welsh castles, begun in 1295 after the rising of Madog ap Llywelyn. Money ran short and work petered out by the 1320s, leaving the towers below their planned height. The borough became the main port of Anglesey.
A Norman ringwork of the early 12th century, rebuilt in stone as a concentric castle in the late 13th and 14th centuries. The Lord Rhys captured it in 1159.

Henry III began the stone castle about 1223 against Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, replacing the nearby timber castle of Hen Domen. It withstood attacks in 1228, 1231 and 1245. The treaty that recognised Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales was sealed at the nearby ford in 1267.
A castle built by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1273 on a ridge above the Severn, in defiance of the king and facing royal Montgomery. Roger Mortimer took it in 1277 after a two-week siege.
A late medieval fortress-palace in Gwent. Sir William ap Thomas built the moated Great Tower about 1435 and his son William Herbert, earl of Pembroke, enlarged it.

A Welsh princely residence of Dafydd ap Gruffudd, whose attack on Hawarden in 1282 set off Edward I’s final war. Henry de Lacy then built a large castle and walled town on the site; the half-built castle was captured in the rising of 1294.
A motte and bailey in the Cynllaith valley, the chief home of Owain Glyndŵr. A poem of about 1390 praises its fine timber hall on a green mound; it was burnt in 1403 and has no later history.
A hilltop castle above Llangollen, built inside an Iron Age hillfort by the rulers of northern Powys in the 1260s and burnt by its own garrison before Edward I’s army in 1277.
The first Cistercian abbey in Wales, founded in 1131 on the Wye. The great church was begun in 1269. The abbey surrendered in 1536 in the first round of the dissolution.

A Cistercian abbey in the Ceredigion uplands, founded in 1164 by a Norman lord and soon taken under the patronage of the Lord Rhys. The monks entered their new church in 1201. Welsh princes were buried here and it supported the Welsh cause; it closed by 1539.
A Cistercian abbey near Llangollen, founded in 1201 by Madog ap Gruffudd, prince of northern Powys, and named after the nearby Pillar of Eliseg. It was dissolved in 1537.
Founded in 1130 by the Norman knight Richard de Granville; by the late 13th century one of the wealthiest abbeys in Wales.

A Cistercian abbey founded about 1147 and dissolved in 1536, thought to stand on an earlier monastic site: early Christian carved stones were found around it. The western part of the nave survives as the parish church.
An abbey near Holywell on the Dee estuary, founded in 1131 and much rebuilt in the 13th century. Wat’s Dyke reaches the estuary close by.

The castle at the mouth of the Tawe was founded in or soon after 1106 as the head of the Norman lordship of Gower; a borough and port grew beside it. The first castle was earth and timber, rebuilt in stone probably between 1221 and 1284.
A castle founded about 1110 by Tancred, a Fleming, at the tidal limit of the Western Cleddau. The town below it became one of the largest and richest in medieval Wales.
Bernard de Neufmarché defeated the king of Brycheiniog near here in 1093 and built a castle and a Benedictine priory (now the cathedral) at the meeting of the Usk and Honddu. A walled town followed.
A market town on the Welsh side of the border, first recorded in the 12th century. It was never a chartered walled borough but by the 16th century was among the most populous towns in Wales.
Edward I’s brother Edmund began the castle and borough in 1277, at first called Llanbadarn. Owain Glyndŵr held it from 1404 to 1408.

William fitz Osbern built a castle where the Monnow meets the Wye soon after 1066; a priory and walled town followed. Henry V was born in the castle in 1386 or 1387. A Roman fort, Blestium, had stood here.
A small market town in the Dyfi valley, with a market charter of 1291. By tradition Owain Glyndŵr was crowned Prince of Wales and held a parliament here in 1404.

In 1081 Gruffudd ap Cynan, returning from exile in Ireland, and Rhys ap Tewdwr defeated and killed Trahaearn ap Caradog, Caradog ap Gruffudd and Meilyr ap Rhiwallon. The victory secured Gwynedd for Gruffudd’s line and Deheubarth for Rhys’s.

In 1136 Owain and Cadwaladr of Gwynedd with Gruffudd ap Rhys routed a Norman and Flemish army near Cardigan; many of the defeated drowned in the Teifi. It was the largest Welsh victory of the rising that followed Henry I’s death.

On 11 December 1282 the king’s forces with Roger Mortimer and Gruffudd ap Gwenwynwyn came on the Welsh army without warning near Builth. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, and his leading men were killed; native rule in Wales ended within months.
On 22 June 1402 Owain Glyndŵr’s men defeated the levies of Herefordshire at Pilleth in Maelienydd and captured Edmund Mortimer, who then joined Glyndŵr’s cause.
In 1255 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd defeated his brothers Owain and Dafydd and became sole ruler of Gwynedd west of the Conwy, the first step toward his principality.

The ditch and bank were dug about 3000 BCE and the great stones set up about 2500 BCE. The bluestones were rearranged two or three centuries later and the last known digging, the Y and Z holes, dates to 1800-1500 BCE.
A very large late Neolithic settlement beside the Avon, later enclosed by Britain's largest henge. It is linked to the building of the sarsen phase at Stonehenge, 3 km away.
The largest stone circle in Britain, inside a huge henge ditch, built and altered from about 2850 to about 2200 BCE. Its monuments were abandoned around 1800 BCE.
The largest artificial prehistoric mound in Europe, probably raised over a short period between about 2470 and 2350 BCE. Its purpose is unknown.
One of the largest Neolithic chambered tombs in Britain, built around 3650 BCE, used for at least a thousand years and blocked with great sarsens around 2000 BCE.
The largest known Neolithic causewayed enclosure, three rings of interrupted ditch on a low hill near Avebury.
A chalk spur in Dorset used twice: as a large early Neolithic enclosure complex and, three thousand years later, as a multivallate hillfort.
Among the earliest flint mines in Britain, with over 200 shafts on the South Downs, later enclosed by one of the largest hillforts in Sussex.
High fell-side quarries whose green volcanic stone was made into polished axes found all over Britain.
A ring of 38 stones among the Lake District fells, probably raised in the late Neolithic.
Three large henges in a line across the Ure-Swale plain, the largest ritual complex between the Thames and Orkney.
A henge and recumbent stone circle on the White Peak limestone plateau.
A field of more than 400 late Neolithic flint mine shafts in the Norfolk Breckland, worked from about 2600 to about 2100 BCE.
A ring of 55 split oak posts around an inverted tree stump, built on a saltmarsh. Tree rings show the timbers were felled in 2049 BCE.
A kilometre-long post alignment and timber platform across the fen edge near Peterborough, built in stages between about 1365 and 967 BCE and used for ritual deposits long afterwards.
A small late Bronze Age settlement of round houses on stilts over a fen channel, destroyed by fire very soon after it was built and preserved in the silt.
The best-known of the Bronze Age enclosed settlements on Dartmoor, part of a moor then divided by long field boundaries (reaves).
A 110 m stylised horse cut into the chalk of the Berkshire Downs, with an early Iron Age hillfort on the ridge above.
The largest hillfort in Britain. In the middle Iron Age (about 400-120 BCE) it was the main settlement of southern Dorset; by the Roman invasion it was almost empty.
The most thoroughly excavated hillfort in Britain, with streets of round houses and thousands of grain storage pits; perhaps 200-350 people lived inside.
A Somerset hillfort reoccupied on a large scale in the late 5th and 6th centuries, one of the strongest pieces of evidence for post-Roman British lordship in the south-west.
A waterlogged Iron Age village in the Somerset Levels, exceptionally well preserved.
The main known port of late Iron Age Britain before Caesar: Italian wine, glass and figs came in, and metals went out to Armorica.
Some 300 hectares of earthworks in North Yorkshire, probably the seat of the Brigantian rulers who were clients of Rome until about 69 CE.

Founded about 47-50 CE, burned in 60/61, the largest town of Roman Britain, then almost deserted for two centuries. From the late 9th century it grew back inside its Roman walls and by 1377 had about three times as many taxpayers as any other English town.
The chief centre of late Iron Age Britain, then a legionary fortress and the first Roman colonia, burned by Boudica in 60/61. It was tenth among English towns in the 1377 poll tax.
The third great town of Roman Britain by tradition, burned by Boudica in 61. The medieval abbey and town grew on the hill outside the Roman walls, around the supposed grave of Britain's first martyr.

Founded as a legionary fortress in 71. Two emperors died here and Constantine was proclaimed here in 306. It was the Viking capital of the north from 866/7 to 954 and the second town of England in 1377.
A fortress of about 60 CE turned into a colonia for veterans, probably in 86. It revived under Danish rule and stood among the four or five largest English towns from Domesday to the 13th century.
A colonia founded under Nerva at the lowest crossing of the Severn. It was eighth by Russell's Domesday estimate and seventeenth in 1377.
Begun in the mid 70s as the largest legionary fortress in Britain and held until the late 4th or early 5th century. Refortified in 907, it became the seat of a Norman marcher earldom.
Founded as a military base about 47 and refounded as a city in the 90s. At 78 hectares it was one of the largest cities of Roman Britain. It was never built over.
An Iron Age centre founded about 20-10 BCE which became a Roman town and, unusually, was never reoccupied.
Widely believed to be the landing place of 43 CE and long the formal gateway to Britain. The town was cleared after 250 for a fort, rebuilt in stone in 275-290.
Roman capital of Kent, then from 597 the centre of the English church. It was fourteenth in the 1377 poll tax and tenth by wealth in the 1520s.
Roman Venta, refounded by Alfred with a new street grid and the largest burh in the Burghal Hidage. It was second only to London at Domesday but thirtieth in the 1377 poll tax.
Civitas capital of the Dobunni and, on the usual reconstruction, capital of the 4th-century province of Britannia Prima.
A sanctuary and bathing complex around the hot spring, not an ordinary town. The Roman Baths' own timeline has the buildings collapsing by about 500 and a Saxon church founded in 675.
The western end of the Fosse Way, held successively as fortress, Roman town, burh and cathedral city. It ranked 24th in 1377 and 6th in the 1520s.
Civitas capital of the Corieltauvi and later one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. It ranked eighteenth in 1377.
Roman capital of the client kingdom of Togidubnus and its successor civitas, refortified as a burh and made a bishop's seat in 1075.
The largest Roman residence known north of the Alps, commonly linked to the client king Togidubnus.
Founded about 70 CE, after nearby Maiden Castle had emptied.
A small Roman town laid out in Iceni territory after the Boudican revolt and never built over.
The northernmost civitas capital of Roman Britain: a trading settlement from about 70, laid out as a planned town about 120 and walled in stone in the late 2nd century.
The Roman town at the west end of the frontier. It was taken into the English kingdom only in 1092.
Usually taken to be the civitas centre of the Parisi, on the strength of one theatre inscription.
A walled small town at the centre of the Nene Valley pottery industry; the earliest Christian silver plate from the Roman empire was found here.
A Roman fort and town at the Swale crossing; Bede names it as a place where Paulinus baptised.
The most northerly town of the Roman empire, where Dere Street crossed the Tyne.
A fort built before Hadrian's Wall and rebuilt nine times. Its ink writing tablets, of about 100 CE, are the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.
Built within a decade of 122 for an 800-strong infantry regiment, and held to the end of the 4th century.
Built about 124 for a 500-strong cavalry regiment and occupied until the Roman army left Britain.
A Wall fort where large timber halls show a community staying on under local leaders after Roman pay stopped.
The sea port of Hadrian's Wall, turned into a granary depot for the Severan campaigns in Scotland.
The shortest crossing to Gaul. The Roman lighthouse of about 130 still stands inside the castle, whose great tower Henry II built in 1179-89; the castle held out against a French siege in 1216-17.
The best preserved Roman fort north of the Alps, reused as a burh and a medieval castle.
Built about 290 (tree-ring date). William of Normandy landed here on 28 September 1066 and a medieval castle grew within the Roman circuit.
A shore fort overlooking the wide estuary that then covered the lower Yare and Waveney.
An early Saxon Shore fort guarding the channel that then made Thanet an island; a Kentish minster was founded in it in 669.
Where Watling Street crossed the Medway. England's second-oldest see was founded here in 604.
A Roman fort, then for centuries a minor place. It is included to show how small the later industrial cities still were in 1625.
A Roman fort site that became the castle and shire town of a county palatine.
Lead was being mined on Mendip under army control within six years of the invasion: stamped ingots are dated to 49 CE.
Centre of the Peak District lead field, worked in the Roman period and recorded again from the 8th century and in Domesday.
A defended headland with more imported 5th-7th century Mediterranean pottery than any other site in Britain, probably a seat of the rulers of Dumnonia.
A fully excavated early English village, standing here for the thousands of small farming settlements of the 5th to 7th centuries.
A mound cemetery above the Deben. The great ship burial of about 625 is most often thought to be that of King Raedwald.
Named by Bede as a royal residence; excavation since 2008 has found a large, rich settlement 6 km from Sutton Hoo.
One of the four great trading towns (wics) of 7th-9th century England and continuously a town ever since. It was 27th in 1377, 8th in the 1520s and 7th in the 1662 hearth tax.
Hamwic, on the west bank of the Itchen, held perhaps 2,000-3,000 people at its height about 700-850. The walled medieval port grew a little to the south-west.
The successor to Richborough as the main port of east Kent, until its haven silted in the 15th and 16th centuries.
A Northumbrian royal centre below the hillfort of Yeavering Bell. In 627 Paulinus spent 36 days here baptising in the River Glen.
The citadel of Bernicia, traditionally taken by Ida in 547, and the base of the English earls who survived north of the Tyne after the Vikings took York.

Founded in 635 from Iona. Cuthbert died here in 687 and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made about 710-725. Raided on 8 June 793, left for good in 875, and refounded as a cell of Durham by 1122 until its closure in 1537.
Benedict Biscop's 'one monastery in two places', the home of Bede (died 735) and for a time the most learned house in northern Europe.
Founded about 657 and the scene of the synod of 664 that settled the dating of Easter. Abandoned in the 9th century, refounded about 1078 and suppressed in 1539.
Wilfrid's church, built with stone from Roman Corbridge; its 7th-century crypt survives.
A Northumbrian monastery whose 7th-century crypt survives under the later minster.
Cuthbert's relics came to rest here in 995 after the community's long wandering from Lindisfarne by way of Chester-le-Street.
A minster town which grew into one of the larger towns of medieval England before its cloth trade moved to the West Riding.
Mercia had no fixed capital, but its kings issued more charters at Tamworth than anywhere else. A 9th-century watermill has been excavated here.
A Mercian royal mausoleum. The Great Army wintered here in 873-4, and a D-shaped earthwork and a mass grave of at least 264 people have been excavated.
The Great Army's camp of 872-3 covered some 55 hectares, larger than most towns of the day.
The church centre of Mercia and, for sixteen years under Offa, the seat of a third English archbishop.
Chosen as the bishop's seat for the kingdom of the Hwicce in 679-680. It was 26th in 1377 and 12th in the 1662 hearth tax.
The English frontier town against south Wales, burned by a Welsh and Irish force in 1055. Tenth by Russell's Domesday estimate, 21st in 1377.
The chief town of the middle March, 19th in the 1377 poll tax and 14th in 1662.
The richest abbey in England at Domesday and again at the Dissolution. Its last abbot was hanged on the Tor in 1539.
A hilltop abbey and burh; King Aethelstan was buried here in 939.
Bishop's seat for Wessex west of Selwood from 705 until the Council of London of 1075 moved it to Old Sarum.
A cathedral city that never grew large: the church, not trade, was its reason for being.
The island fort from which Alfred rallied Wessex in the spring of 878 before Edington.
Rated at 2,400 hides, the same as Winchester. William crossed the Thames here in 1066. Its Saxon ramparts survive.
A West Saxon burh of 1,600 hides whose earth ramparts still enclose the town on three sides.
A burh of 700 hides and the home of the wealthiest house of nuns in medieval England, dissolved in 1539.
A burh of 1,300 hides and the chief town of Norman Sussex; about 2,000 people at Domesday.
A burh of 500 hides which gave its name to the battle fought 10 km inland.
A late Saxon border burh of 1,400 hides which Darby put at about 5,000 people in 1066. Schools gathered here in the 12th century; it was sixteenth in 1377.
A river-crossing town where scholars fleeing Oxford settled in 1209; they had a chancellor by 1226. It was 22nd in 1377.
Not a Roman town: it grew from the 10th century and Darby gives it about 6,500 people in 1066. Sixth in 1377, it was second only to London in the 1520s and in 1662.
Sixth largest town in Domesday England and briefly a cathedral city, then eclipsed by Norwich.
One of the richest abbeys in England, built over the body of the East Anglian king killed by the Danes in 869. Fifteenth in 1377.
A fen-island monastery that became one of the great cathedrals; 23rd in the 1377 poll tax.
A fen-edge abbey whose monks kept the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle going until 1154.
A Danish army base taken by Aethelflaed in 917.
One of the Five Boroughs; 29th in the 1377 poll tax.
A Danelaw borough which Darby put at about 3,000 people in 1086.
A favoured meeting place of 12th-century kings and councils; 28th in 1377.
Listed at 2,400 hides in the later Burghal Hidage manuscripts.
A hillfort of about 400 BCE reused for a mint in 1003, a Norman castle and a cathedral (see moved here 1075). The clergy left for the new city of Salisbury in the 1220s.
Founded in 1220 to replace Old Sarum. It was eighth in the 1377 poll tax and seventh by wealth in the 1520s.
First heard of about 1000. Third in the 1377 poll tax and in the 1520s, and the starting point of English Atlantic voyages from the 1480s.
The great boom town of the 14th-century Midlands; it then lost perhaps half its people between about 1440 and 1520 and was 19th in 1662.
The base of Drake and Hawkins and the port the fleet sailed from against the Armada in 1588.
The outlet for the whole Great Ouse basin. Ninth in 1377 and ninth by wealth in the 1520s.
At its 13th-century peak Boston exported more wool than any other English port. Eleventh in 1377.
A town built on a sandspit that formed across the Roman-period estuary. Twentieth in 1377, eighth in 1662.
One of the largest ports of the east coast in the 12th and 13th centuries. Storms in 1286, 1287, 1328, 1347 and 1362 destroyed most of it and shifted its river mouth.
A 13th-century boom port off Spurn Head which sent members to the parliament of 1295 and was drowned in the winter storms of 1356-62.
Edward I's replacement for Old Winchelsea, which the sea destroyed in 1287. Much of its street grid was never filled.
Bought by Edward I in 1293 as a northern supply port. It was 25th in 1377 and 18th in 1662.
Named from Robert Curthose's castle of 1080. It was 13th in 1377 and 4th in the 1520s, by then sending coal by sea to London.
A Scottish town for most of the Middle Ages, finally taken by England in 1482. It is listed under England only for that last phase.
One of a chain of late 4th-century coastal watchtowers, later a major royal castle.
A minor port until Henry VII built a dry dock here in 1495; the Mary Rose sank offshore in 1545.
A Devon port for the Bordeaux wine trade, privateering and later the Newfoundland fishery.
The chief church of Cornwall after its bishops moved east, and a rallying point of the risings of 1497 and 1549.
A small town transformed by Henry I's abbey of 1121, dissolved in 1539 when its abbot was hanged.
A Suffolk village that briefly paid more tax than York, on the strength of its blue broadcloth.
The second pilgrim shrine of medieval England after Canterbury.
Founded by William about 1071 on the site of his victory, consecrated in 1094 and surrendered in May 1538.
The richest Cistercian house in England, dissolved in 1539.
Founded in March 1132. Under Aelred it held 140 monks and about 500 lay brothers. It was shut down on 3 December 1538.
In 1537 the first of the larger houses to be dissolved by voluntary surrender.
One of the ring of castles William built around London, and a main royal residence from the 12th century.
Begun about 1120. It withstood a six-month siege in 1266, was rebuilt as a palace by John of Gaunt from 1371, and entertained Elizabeth I in 1575.
One of the earliest stone castles in England and a favourite stronghold of King John.
A Lacy and Mortimer castle which became the administrative capital of Wales and the border counties from 1472.
The strongest castle in Yorkshire.
Built after the Harrying of the North to hold the lands of the former English earl; among the oldest stone castles in England.
The stronghold of the Percy earls of Northumberland, the dominant family of the far north.
Where Mary Tudor gathered her supporters and was proclaimed queen in 1553.
A favourite residence of Henry II and Henry III; the Constitutions of Clarendon were issued here in 1164.
The best surviving Tudor royal palace; the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 commissioned the King James Bible.
Begun in 1538 to rival the French king's châteaux; pulled down in the 1680s.
Still a town of a few hundred people in 1625. Included to show how small the later great port was.
A village with a borough attached until woollen cloth-making made it a town in the 16th century; incorporated in 1626.
Granted a market in 1166; by the 1530s Leland heard its smiths from the road.
The main cloth town of the north-west.
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says the West Saxons killed three British kings here and took Gloucester, Cirencester and Bath.
Egbert of Wessex defeated Beornwulf of Mercia; Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex passed to Wessex and Mercian dominance ended.
In May 878 Alfred defeated Guthrum's army, which then accepted baptism and withdrew to East Anglia.
Aethelstan defeated the allied kings of Dublin, Scotland and Strathclyde, securing the new kingdom of the English.
Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex was killed fighting a Viking fleet on 10 or 11 August 991; payments of tribute followed.
Edmund Ironside crossed the Thames at Brentford two days after relieving London and drove Cnut's army off, at heavy cost to his own men.
On 18 October 1016 Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside; Edmund died weeks later and Cnut took the whole kingdom.
On 20 September 1066 Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar outside York.
On 25 September 1066 Harold Godwinson surprised and killed Harald Hardrada and Tostig.
On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold. Battle Abbey was founded on the site about 1071.
On 22 August 1138 a northern English army raised by Archbishop Thurstan defeated David I of Scotland near Northallerton.
Simon de Montfort captured Henry III and the Lord Edward on 14 May 1264 and ruled in the king's name for a year.
The Lord Edward trapped and killed Simon de Montfort on 4 August 1265.
A northern English army defeated and captured David II of Scotland outside Durham on 17 October 1346.
A Scottish raiding army defeated the Percys in a moonlit fight in Redesdale.
Henry IV defeated the Percy rebellion and Henry 'Hotspur' Percy was killed, on 21 July 1403.
A street fight on 22 May 1455 in which Richard of York captured Henry VI; usually counted as the opening of the Wars of the Roses.
Fought in snow on Palm Sunday, 29 March 1461. Edward IV's victory secured him the throne; it is often called the largest and bloodiest battle on English soil.
On Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471, Edward IV defeated and killed Warwick 'the Kingmaker' in fog north of Barnet.
On 4 May 1471 Edward IV destroyed the last Lancastrian army; Edward, Prince of Wales, was killed.
On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated Richard III, the last English king to die in battle.
Henry VII defeated the Yorkist army backing Lambert Simnel on 16 June 1487, the last battle of the Wars of the Roses.
On 9 September 1513 the Earl of Surrey defeated a Scottish invasion; James IV and much of the Scottish nobility were killed.
Mining resumed here in the late 17th century, after this timeline ends.
Large-scale mining began in 1768, after this timeline ends.

The road from the invasion base at Richborough through Canterbury and Rochester to the Thames crossing at London: the first main road of Roman Britain, laid out in the years after AD 43.

The north-west frontier of the Roman empire for nearly 300 years: a wall 80 Roman miles long from the Tyne to the Solway, built by the army on Hadrian’s orders after his visit in AD 122, with forts, milecastles and turrets. It was given up about AD 142 when the frontier moved north to the Antonine Wall, and reoccupied some twenty years later.
The road added behind Hadrian’s Wall when it was recommissioned about AD 160, linking the forts and milecastles.

A bank up to 2.5 m high with a ditch on the Welsh side, the longest earthwork in Britain, marking the western edge of Mercia. Asser, writing about 893, credits it to King Offa (757-796); English Heritage places the work in the 780s.
Lengths of bank on the English side of the Wye gorge, from Sedbury Cliffs on the Severn to near Redbrook and English Bicknor, long treated as the southern end of Offa’s Dyke.
A bank with a ditch on its west side, running about 60 km from Basingwerk on the Dee estuary south past Wrexham and Oswestry to the river Morda at Maesbury, a few kilometres east of Offa’s Dyke.
A massive bank and north-facing ditch running some 20 km along the crest of the Marlborough Downs from Morgan’s Hill to Savernake Forest. The name means ‘Woden’s dyke’.
A smaller, broken earthwork south of Bristol and Bath, from the hillfort of Maes Knoll by Stantonbury to Odd Down above Bath.
A straight bank and ditch about 12 km long from the fen edge at Reach to the wooded clay at Woodditton, the largest of several dykes barring the chalk corridor of the Icknield Way.

The chalk ridge route from the Avebury area along the Berkshire Downs to the Thames at Goring, and on along the Chiltern scarp (as the Icknield Way) to Ivinghoe Beacon, passing Barbury, Uffington and Segsbury hillforts. National Trails describe it as in use for at least 5,000 years.

The main medieval road from London to the north, by Barnet, Hatfield, Baldock, Stamford, Grantham, Newark, Doncaster, Boroughbridge, Durham and Newcastle to Berwick, with York reached by a branch from near Wetherby or Ferrybridge. Kings and armies used it throughout the Scottish wars.

The boundary between Wales and England as fixed by the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-6 and 1542-3, which assigned each marcher lordship to a Welsh or an English county. It runs from the Dee estuary to the Severn, near but seldom on Offa’s Dyke.

The people of south-east Wales, who fought Rome from about AD 48 until their conquest in the mid 70s. Under Roman rule they formed a self-governing community with its centre at Venta Silurum (Caerwent), which lasted to the end of the Roman period. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary.

The people of south-west Wales, whose Roman-period centre was Moridunum (Carmarthen). Their name survived in the early medieval kingdom of Dyfed. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary.

The people of central and north-west Wales. Agricola crushed their rising in AD 77 and founded Segontium afterwards. No Roman-period town or self-governing community is known for them. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder: nothing is heard of them after Ptolemy (about AD 150).

The people of north-east Wales, attacked by the Roman governor Ostorius Scapula about AD 48. Lead ingots from Flintshire of the AD 70s are stamped with their name. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

The kingdom of north-west Wales, with courts at Deganwy and Aberffraw. It became the strongest Welsh power under Rhodri Mawr (844-878), Gruffudd ap Cynan (died 1137), Owain Gwynedd and the two Llywelyns, and ended with Edward I’s conquest in 1282-3. The polygon is indicative for about 1200-1240 under Llywelyn ap Iorwerth: Gwynedd above and below the Conwy with Anglesey, Llŷn, Meirionnydd and Penllyn. The eastern part (the Perfeddwlad, between Conwy and Dee) changed hands repeatedly. The start date is conventional; the dynasty’s origin legend (Cunedda) is not history.

The kingdom of the central borderland. Its early extent reached further east, into what became Shropshire, before Mercian expansion and the building of Offa’s Dyke. Rhodri Mawr took it over in 855. It was divided for good after the death of Madog ap Maredudd in 1160. The polygon is indicative for about 1100-1160; it is not a surveyed boundary. The start date is conventional.

Northern Powys after the division of 1160, ruled from Castell Dinas Brân in the later 13th century; its princes founded Valle Crucis in 1201. It was broken up into marcher lordships (Bromfield and Yale, Chirk) after 1282-3. Only the Valle Crucis foundation is from a fetched source; the rest is general knowledge.

Southern Powys after the division of 1160, centred on Welshpool. Its ruler Gruffudd ap Gwenwynwyn submitted to Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1263, defected in 1274 and fought for Edward I; his heirs kept it as the marcher lordship of Powis.

The kingdom of south-west Wales, heir to the Roman-period Demetae, with a dynasty of partly Irish origin. Hywel Dda acquired it by marriage and joined it to Seisyllwg about 920 to form Deheubarth. The polygon is indicative for about 800. The start date is conventional.

A small kingdom on Cardigan Bay between the Dyfi and the Teifi, by tradition founded by Ceredig. About 730 its king Seisyll is said to have annexed Ystrad Tywi, creating the larger kingdom later called Seisyllwg. The polygon follows the later county and is indicative. Dates are traditional. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

Ceredigion together with Ystrad Tywi (the Tywi valley). On the death of its king Gwgon in 872 it came under Rhodri Mawr; his grandson Hywel Dda joined it to Dyfed about 920 to form Deheubarth. The name ‘Seisyllwg’ appears only in later texts and some historians doubt it was used at the time; the start date is traditional.

The kingdom of the south-west, formed about 920 when Hywel Dda united Dyfed and Seisyllwg. The Normans overran most of it after 1093; Rhys ap Gruffudd (the Lord Rhys) rebuilt it between 1155 and his death in 1197, after which it split among his descendants, who lost their last lands in 1277-87. The polygon is indicative for the Lord Rhys’s rule about 1170-1197: Ceredigion, Ystrad Tywi and parts of Dyfed, excluding the Norman lordships of Pembroke and Gower.

The kingdom between the Tawe and the Usk. In the 10th century, united with Gwent under Morgan Hen (died 974), it came to be called Morgannwg, the origin of ‘Glamorgan’. The Norman Robert fitz Hamon conquered the lowlands about 1091-3. The polygon is indicative for about 950 and excludes Gwent. The start date is conventional. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

The kingdom between the Usk and the Wye, named after Venta Silurum (Caerwent). It was at times joined with Glywysing. William fitz Osbern began its conquest from Chepstow after 1067. The polygon is indicative for about 1000. The start and end dates are approximate.

A small kingdom in the upper Usk valley with a dynasty claiming Irish descent. Its king built the Llangorse crannog about 890; a Mercian army destroyed it in 916. Bernard de Neufmarché conquered the kingdom in 1093 and it became the lordship of Brecon. The polygon is indicative for about 900. The start date is conventional; the conquest date is from general knowledge.

Rhodri became king of Gwynedd in 844, took Powys in 855 and Seisyllwg in 872, so that for a few years one king ruled most of Wales outside the south-east and Dyfed. He was killed fighting the English; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives 877, other reckonings 878. His sons divided the lands. No boundary is drawn because none is known.

Hywel held Seisyllwg from 920 and Dyfed by marriage, and on the death of Idwal Foel in 942 took Gwynedd (and with it Powys), ruling all Wales except Morgannwg and Gwent until his death in 950. The Welsh law-books are attributed to him, though no manuscript is earlier than the 13th century. His kingdom broke up at his death.

value_text: realm: Kingdom of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn
detail: King of Gwynedd and Powys from 1039, Gruffudd took Deheubarth in 1055 and Morgannwg soon after: the only king ever to rule the whole of Wales, with land east of Offa’s Dyke as well. Harold Godwinson’s campaign of 1063 broke his power and he was killed by his own men (5 August 1063 in the usual reckoning; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography’s revised article argues for 1064). The polygon is modern Wales, used as an indication; his holdings beyond the dyke are not drawn.

value_text: principality: Principality of Wales (Llywelyn ap Gruffudd)
detail: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took the homage of the other Welsh lords in 1258 and styled himself Prince of Wales; Henry III recognised the title and the principality in the Treaty of Montgomery (1267). Edward I’s war of 1276-7 cut it back to Gwynedd west of the Conwy; Llywelyn was killed in December 1282 and his brother Dafydd captured in 1283. The polygon is a rough indication of the lands under Llywelyn’s lordship at the treaty in 1267: Gwynedd, both parts of Powys, Builth, Brecon, Gwerthrynion and the Welsh lords of Deheubarth. Its southern and eastern edges were contested and are not well defined.

entity_name: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth)
value_text: principality: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth)
detail: After the conquest the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) annexed Llywelyn’s principality to the English crown and set up counties on the English model, governed from Caernarfon. From 1301 the principality was usually granted to the king’s eldest son. Flintshire, also created in 1284, was attached to Chester and is not drawn. The polygon is indicative: the three north-western shires as they stood from 1284. The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-6 ended the legal distinction between Principality and March.

entity_name: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen)
value_text: principality: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen)
detail: The southern part of the crown’s principality: the counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen, governed from Carmarthen and built up from royal lands held since the 1240s and the forfeited lands of the princes of Deheubarth (1277-87). The polygon is indicative for about 1300; medieval Carmarthenshire was smaller than the later county and its edges against the marcher lordships of Kidwelly, Llandovery and Emlyn are approximate. The make-up of these counties is from general knowledge.

The belt of some forty or more lordships along the border and across south Wales, conquered piecemeal by Norman lords from 1067 (Chepstow, Montgomery, Brecon, Glamorgan, Pembroke) and enlarged after 1282 with new lordships in the north-east (Denbigh, Ruthin, Bromfield and Yale, Chirk). Each lord held royal powers in his lordship and the king’s writ did not run there. The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-6 abolished these powers and divided the lordships among new and existing shires. No polygon is drawn: the March was not one territory, and its extent changed with every war.

Owain Glyndŵr attacked Ruthin on 16 September 1400 and took the title Prince of Wales. After Bryn Glas (1402) and the capture of Aberystwyth and Harlech (1404) he controlled most of Wales, made a treaty with France and planned a parliament and an independent Welsh church. Defeats from 1405 and the loss of Aberystwyth and Harlech (1408-9) ended his rule; he still raided in 1410 and is not heard of after 1412. The end date is nominal: he never surrendered and probably died about 1415-16. No polygon is drawn because control shifted from year to year.

value_text: principality: Wales (shired and united with England)
detail: The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-6 and 1542-3 united Wales with England, abolished the powers of the marcher lords, created the counties of Monmouth, Brecknock, Radnor, Montgomery and Denbigh beside the older ones, gave Wales members of Parliament and made English the language of the courts. The acts also fixed the boundary with England. The polygon is the modern outline of Wales, generalised; it includes Monmouthshire, which the 1542-3 act placed under the Westminster courts and whose status was long ambiguous. The fetched legislation.gov.uk pages confirm the two acts and their dates; the summary of their provisions is from general knowledge.

value_text: kingdom: Kingdom of the South Saxons
detail: Traditional foundation by Aelle in 477; converted by Wilfrid from 681; under Mercia 771-796, subject to Wessex from about 827 and fully absorbed in 860. The polygon is the kingdom of about 700, bounded inland by the Weald forest. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. value_text: kingdom: Kingdom of the East Saxons
detail: Founded in the 6th century (527 is a traditional and uncertain date). It ceded itself to Wessex in 825. The polygon is the kingdom of about 650, when it still included Middlesex, London and much of Hertfordshire; Mercia took those by the mid 8th century. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

value_text: kingdom: Kingdom of the East Angles
detail: Organised in the first half of the 6th century and ruled by the Wuffingas, of whom Raedwald (died about 624) was the most powerful. King Edmund was killed by the Danes in 869. The polygon is the kingdom of about 700: Norfolk and Suffolk, with the Fens as its western march. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines.
